Because Ms. Barnes chose to be a mandatory supporter instead of a mandatory reporter, this child and her siblings might never be among the 53% of Black children who are subjected to the trauma of a child abuse investigation before they turn 18. They probably won't be forced into foster care, where studies find abuse in 1/4 to 1/3 of foster homes, and many other studies find that, in typical cases, foster children fare worse even than comparably maltreated children left in their own homes.

Just 27% of actively managed U.S. large-cap equity funds beat their benchmark passive-fund alternatives in the 12 months ended June 30, according to Morningstar data that compares returns after fees. That is actually an improvement over stock-picking funds’ long-term track record. In the decade through June, just 13% of active large-cap funds beat their benchmarks. 

There have been many studies since 2010 that confirmed this underperformance by active managers.

But the S&P 500 and Nasdaq-100 are weighted by market value, and outsize gains from a handful of superstar companies continue to drive returns. The S&P 500’s 10 largest companies represent more than 40% of its value, according to Dow Jones Market Data—the highest concentration since the 1960s.

But the current environment presents an unprecedented challenge of high concentration in just a few stocks.

While this works well for passive investors in these concentrated funds as AI and tech stocks rise, the underperperformance could be devastating if what many believe is an AI/tech bubble bursts.

Investors must not only consider the outperformance of their funds but also the incremental risk assumed for each 100 basis point increase  in return over the risk-free rate.  The  Sharpe ratio is the most commonly used measure of incremental risk assumed per unit of excess return.  No mention of that here.

There is some simple arithmetic behind the failure of active management to beat indices.       All of the portfolios which are not indexed to the entire market taken together match the index of the entire market. (The whole market minus the index funds is just equal to the index.)   Furthermore, any excess profits that can come from active trading are at the expense of other active traders.    (Since passive investors don't trade, they don't lose money to traders.)

      Consequently, the net returns all  stock picking funds net of costs and fees are just equal to the returns of the broad market index minus all of the costs, fees, and market making profits earned by Wall Street.

But the worst are the orphaned male calves who are malnourished, don't get colostrum from even a first nursing and have damaged bones and hooves and become quite sick.

The lucky ones end up at a place like ours.

I'm taking wonderful care of horses and helping do PT with Gabriel.  He was essentially left to starve on a dairy farm.  He had a fractured leg and injured hoof.  He's had surgery and in a cast and gets walked to build bone and muscle strength in his injured leg.

He loves being scratched, petted, gives kisses, wants to nurse on everyone and is such a sweet boy.  He'll eventually join Ebb, Owen, Romeo (our other lucky boys) and once he gets stronger and cast is removed, he'll have Flo as his foster mom.

Yes, I've galloped on beaches in SW Ireland.  It was magical.

What happens to jockeys or horses when their racing days are over isn't pretty.  Last pic is a female calf.

Roughly speaking, I lived in Hawaii for the first 30 years and in Guam for the last 30 years.  Surviving multiple typhoons over that period means we had to prepare for many more that missed.
Homes and buildings in Hawaii are not designed for hurricane living.  Installing a roof or window to withstand hurricane force wind speeds is only part of home defense.  Imagine your neighbor’s patio umbrella going airborne at that speed hitting a bedroom window - a protective shutter helps but not if your family is sitting on the other side of that window.  
There is also prep for water leakage. Louvered windows are great for Hawaii weather, but it won’t help if rain is traveling horizontally at 70 mph.  I learned about capillary effect in my first typhoon, when rain was coming through the center of the knob on our front door.  It’s easy to imagine if you’re on the freeway and stick your hand out the window. 
On another note, it’s my impression that typhoon forecasting became excellent but has become noticeably worse over the last year. 
Godspeed, Hawaii.
